lead: A dilute solute does not see a pure-liquid environment. It sees solvent, so its vapour pressure is not x<sub>i</sub> P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup>. Henry's law replaces P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup> with a measured slope H<sub>i</sub>: partial pressure equals mole fraction times H<sub>i</sub>. This chapter shows why H<sub>i</sub> is the limiting slope at x<sub>i</sub> → 0, how it links to the infinite-dilution activity coefficient, how temperature and pressure shift it, and how a dilute binary uses Henry for the solute and Raoult for the solvent. Dissolved oxygen in boiler feed water and CO₂ in soft drinks are the working examples.
prereq: You need Raoult's law and modified Raoult's law and the standard states from phase equilibria of pure components and mixtures.

sections.h3: Why the solute needs its own slope

blocks.text: Raoult's law describes the solvent of a dilute solution well and the solute badly. A gas molecule in water is surrounded almost entirely by water molecules. It has no pure-liquid environment, so its pure vapour pressure P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup> is the wrong reference. Henry's law fixes this by replacing the pure-liquid vapour pressure with a measured slope.
p<sub>i</sub> = x<sub>i</sub> H<sub>i</sub>    or    f<sub>i</sub> = x<sub>i</sub> k<sub>i</sub>
blocks.where: p<sub>i</sub> is the partial pressure of solute i in the gas (Pa); x<sub>i</sub> is its mole fraction in the liquid; H<sub>i</sub> is Henry's constant on the mole-fraction scale (Pa or bar). f<sub>i</sub> is fugacity and k<sub>i</sub> is Henry's constant on the fugacity basis, in the same units as f<sub>i</sub>.

blocks.text: H<sub>i</sub> is the limiting slope of the p<sub>i</sub> against x<sub>i</sub> curve as x<sub>i</sub> → 0. It is a property of the solute–solvent pair and of temperature. For CO₂ in water at 298 K, H is about 1670 bar. For O₂ in water it is about 4.4 × 10⁴ bar, some 26 times larger, so oxygen is much less soluble.

The standard state behind H<sub>i</sub> is a hypothetical pure liquid: the solute at x<sub>i</sub> = 1 behaving as it does at infinite dilution. The reference is hypothetical because no real pure liquid solute has that environment. Because of this choice, the solute's activity coefficient approaches 1 as x<sub>i</sub> → 0. The two constants are linked:

blocks.where: γ<sub>i</sub><sup>∞</sup> is the activity coefficient of solute i at infinite dilution; P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup> is the vapour pressure of pure liquid i (Pa).

blocks.text: This ratio can be large. For a gas above its critical temperature, P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup> does not exist at all. Henry's constant is then the only usable reference.

In a binary solution the solvent is nearly pure and the solute is nearly absent. The same measured curve therefore obeys Raoult's law at the solvent end and Henry's law at the solute end. A one-parameter Margules model reproduces both ends with a single constant A:
p₁ = x₁ exp[A(1 − x₁)²] P₁<sup>sat</sup>,    A = ln(H₁ / P₁<sup>sat</sup>)
blocks.where: p₁ is the partial pressure of component 1 (Pa); x₁ is its liquid mole fraction; P₁<sup>sat</sup> is its pure vapour pressure (Pa); H₁ is its Henry constant (Pa); A is a dimensionless Margules constant.

blocks.text: Check the two limits. As x₁ → 1, the exponential becomes 1 and p₁ → P₁<sup>sat</sup>. As x₁ → 0, p₁ ≈ x₁ exp(A) P₁<sup>sat</sup> = x₁ H₁. The Henry line is the tangent at x₁ = 0. The Raoult line p₁ = x₁ P₁<sup>sat</sup> is the tangent at x₁ = 1. The figure uses P₁<sup>sat</sup> = 60 kPa and H₁ = 90 kPa, so A = ln(90/60) = 0.405.

The Henry line is accurate only while the solute is dilute. A common working range is xi below 0.02 to 0.05. Inside that range the solvent still follows Raoult's law: psolvent = xsolvent Psolventsat. This is why a dilute binary uses two standard states at once — Raoult-based for the solvent, Henry-based for the solute. Both are the same fugacity equality from 6.1, just written with different references.
Henry's constant is not a constant. It changes with temperature and, weakly, with pressure. The temperature dependence is:
d ln H<sub>i</sub> / dT = (h̄<sub>i</sub><sup>V</sup> − h̄<sub>i</sub><sup>∞</sup>) / (R T²)
blocks.where: H<sub>i</sub> is Henry's constant (Pa); T is absolute temperature (K); R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹; h̄<sub>i</sub><sup>V</sup> is the partial molar enthalpy of i in the vapour (J mol⁻¹); h̄<sub>i</sub><sup>∞</sup> is the partial molar enthalpy of i at infinite dilution in the liquid (J mol⁻¹).

blocks.text: For most gases in water the right side is positive: dissolving releases heat, so H rises with T and solubility falls. That is why a warm soft drink goes flat. Cold water holds more dissolved oxygen than warm water. Boiler feed water is deaerated because even the small amount of oxygen that remains at high temperature corrodes steel.
d ln H<sub>i</sub> / dP = V̄<sub>i</sub><sup>∞</sup> / (R T)
blocks.where: V̄<sub>i</sub><sup>∞</sup> is the partial molar volume of i at infinite dilution (m³ mol⁻¹); P is pressure (Pa); R and T as above.

blocks.text: V̄<sub>i</sub><sup>∞</sup> is small for gases, so pressure changes H only slightly. The bigger effect of pressure is on the partial pressure itself. A soda bottle at 3 bar of CO₂ holds more dissolved CO₂ than one at 1 bar because x<sub>CO₂</sub> = p<sub>CO₂</sub>/H<sub>CO₂</sub> rises with p<sub>CO₂</sub>.

figure.caption: One curve, two laws: the real partial pressure leaves the origin along the Henry tangent (slope 90 kPa) and reaches x₁ = 1 along the Raoult line (slope 60 kPa), lying between them in the middle (33.2 kPa at x₁ = 0.5). The boxes give the two worked gas solubilities.

spec.aria: Partial pressure against x1 from 0 to 1: a dashed Henry line of slope 90, a dashed Raoult line of slope 60 and a solid real curve that starts along the Henry line and ends at 60 kilopascals on the Raoult line; side boxes give carbon dioxide at 3 bar dissolving to x = 1.80 times 10 to the minus 3 and oxygen from air to 8.6 milligrams per kilogram.

examples.question: Carbon dioxide in water at 298 K has a Henry constant of about 1670 bar on the mole-fraction scale. A soft drink is carbonated at a CO₂ partial pressure of 3.0 bar. Find the mole fraction of dissolved CO₂, and its molality in water.
steps: Henry's law on the mole-fraction scale: p<sub>CO₂</sub> = x<sub>CO₂</sub> H<sub>CO₂</sub>. Rearrange: x<sub>CO₂</sub> = p<sub>CO₂</sub> / H<sub>CO₂</sub>.
Take 1 mol of solution. Then n<sub>CO₂</sub> = 1.796 × 10⁻³ mol and n<sub>water</sub> = 1 − 1.796 × 10⁻³ = 0.998204 mol.
Molality m = n<sub>CO₂</sub> / mass of water = 1.796 × 10⁻³ mol / 0.017983 kg = 0.0999 mol kg⁻¹, about 4.4 g of CO₂ per kg of water.
examples.answer: x<sub>CO₂</sub> = 1.796 × 10⁻³, and the molality of dissolved CO₂ is 0.0999 mol kg⁻¹ (about 4.4 g per kg of water).

examples.question: Boiler feed water at 298 K is in contact with air at 1.013 bar, which is 21 mol % oxygen. Henry's constant for O₂ in water at 298 K is about 4.4 × 10⁴ bar. Find the dissolved O₂ as a mole fraction and in mg per kg of water.
steps: Partial pressure of oxygen: p<sub>O₂</sub> = yP = 0.21 × 1.013 = 0.2127 bar.
One kg of water is 1000/18.015 = 55.51 mol. Because x is tiny, n<sub>O₂</sub> ≈ x × n<sub>water</sub> = 4.83 × 10⁻⁶ × 55.51 = 2.68 × 10⁻⁴ mol.
Mass: 2.68 × 10⁻⁴ mol × 32.00 g/mol = 8.6 × 10⁻³ g = 8.6 mg per kg of water.
examples.answer: x<sub>O₂</sub> = 4.83 × 10⁻⁶, about 8.6 mg of O₂ per kg of water: tiny, but enough to corrode a hot boiler, which is why feed water is deaerated.

traps: Reaching for P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup> for a gas held above its critical temperature, where no vapour pressure exists. Henry's constant is the correct reference there.
Treating H as dimensionless. On the mole-fraction scale it carries pressure units — Pa or bar — and must match the units of p<sub>i</sub>.
Using H<sub>i</sub> and P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup> as if they were the same number. They coincide only when γ<sub>i</sub><sup>∞</sup> = 1, which is rare for gases in water.
Applying p<sub>i</sub> = x<sub>i</sub> H<sub>i</sub> far outside the dilute range. Above x<sub>i</sub> ≈ 0.05 the real curve bends away from the Henry line.
Getting the temperature sign wrong. For most gases in water H rises with T, so solubility falls on warming — the reason warm soda is flat.

quiz.q: State Henry's law for a solute i in a liquid, and give the units of every term.
quiz.a: p<sub>i</sub> = x<sub>i</sub> H<sub>i</sub>, where p<sub>i</sub> is the partial pressure in Pa (or bar), x<sub>i</sub> is the liquid mole fraction (dimensionless), and H<sub>i</sub> is Henry's constant in Pa (or bar) on the mole-fraction scale.

quiz.q: Why is the standard state for a Henry's-law solute called hypothetical?
quiz.a: The reference is the solute at x<sub>i</sub> = 1 with the fugacity it would have if it kept behaving as at infinite dilution all the way to x<sub>i</sub> = 1. In that state the activity coefficient is 1 by construction and the fugacity is H<sub>i</sub>, not P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup>. No real pure liquid solute has that fugacity, so the state is an extrapolation, not a physical liquid.

quiz.q: A gas has H = 2000 bar on the mole-fraction scale. Its partial pressure above the liquid is 2.0 bar. Find x<sub>i</sub>.
A warm cola tastes flat. Explain using the temperature dependence of Henry's constant.
quiz.a: For CO₂ in water, d ln H/dT = (h̄<sup>V</sup> − h̄<sup>∞</sup>)/RT² is positive, so H rises with temperature. At fixed CO₂ partial pressure, x<sub>CO₂</sub> = p<sub>CO₂</sub>/H falls as H rises. The liquid cannot hold as much CO₂, so it escapes and the drink tastes flat.

quiz.q: Why can we not use P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup> for oxygen dissolved in water at 298 K?
quiz.a: Oxygen at 298 K is above its critical temperature, so it has no liquid vapour pressure and P<sub>i</sub><sup>sat</sup> does not exist. Henry's constant is measured for the solute–solvent pair and supplies the needed reference slope.

beyond: Not for the exam. Henry's law appears in environmental engineering as the air–water partitioning constant for pollutants, in CO₂ capture with amine solvents, and in the design of membrane oxygenators. The infinite-dilution activity coefficient γ<sub>i</sub><sup>∞</sup> is measured by gas chromatography: a tiny pulse of solute in a carrier gas gives a retention time that yields H. Salting-out, electrolyte solutions and multicomponent gas solubility need a different treatment. Search 'Henry's law constant compilation', 'infinite dilution activity coefficient' and 'deaeration'.
